claim: Periodontitis is characterized by chronic oral inflammation and uncontrolled tooth supporting alveolar bone resorption.
source: Periodontitis, one of the most common non-communicable diseases, is characterized by chronic oral inflammation and uncontrolled tooth supporting alveolar bone resorption.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about periodontitis presented in the abstract.

claim: A unique fibroblast subpopulation activated to guide oral inflammation (AG fibroblasts) was identified in a single-cell RNA sequencing gingival cell atlas constructed from mouse periodontitis models.
source: Here, we report a unique fibroblast subpopulation activated to guide oral inflammation (AG fibroblasts) identified in a single-cell RNA sequencing gingival cell atlas constructed from the mouse periodontitis models.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: AG fibroblasts localized beneath the gingival epithelium and in the cervical periodontal ligament.
source: AG fibroblasts localized beneath the gingival epithelium and in the cervical periodontal ligament responded to the ligature placement and to the discrete topical application of Toll-like receptor stimulants to mouse maxillary tissue.
evidence: This localization is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AG fibroblasts responded to ligature placement.
source: AG fibroblasts localized beneath the gingival epithelium and in the cervical periodontal ligament responded to the ligature placement and to the discrete topical application of Toll-like receptor stimulants to mouse maxillary tissue.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data showing changes in AG fibroblast gene expression after ligature placement.

claim: AG fibroblasts responded to the discrete topical application of Toll-like receptor stimulants to mouse maxillary tissue.
source: AG fibroblasts localized beneath the gingival epithelium and in the cervical periodontal ligament responded to the ligature placement and to the discrete topical application of Toll-like receptor stimulants to mouse maxillary tissue.
evidence: This is supported by the MTA model experiments with CpG ODN and LPS shown in Figure 4.

claim: The upregulated chemokines and ligands of AG fibroblasts linked to the putative receptors of neutrophils in the early stages of periodontitis.
source: The upregulated chemokines and ligands of AG fibroblasts linked to the putative receptors of neutrophils in the early stages of periodontitis.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of chemokine-receptor interactions shown in Figure 6.

claim: In established chronic inflammation, neutrophils, together with AG fibroblasts, appeared to induce type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s).
source: In the established chronic inflammation, neutrophils, together with AG fibroblasts, appeared to induce type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) that were the primary source of interleukin-17 cytokines.
evidence: This is inferred from scRNA-seq data showing IL-6 and IL-23a expression patterns and ligand-receptor interactions.

claim: ILC3s were the primary source of interleukin-17 cytokines in established chronic inflammation.
source: In the established chronic inflammation, neutrophils, together with AG fibroblasts, appeared to induce type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s) that were the primary source of interleukin-17 cytokines.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data showing Il17a and Il17f expression in ILC3s (Figure 8C).

claim: The comparative analysis of Rag2-/- and Rag2-/-Il2rg-/- mice suggested that ILC3 contributed to the cervical alveolar bone resorption interfacing the gingival inflammation.
source: The comparative analysis of Rag2-/- and Rag2-/-Il2rg-/- mice suggested that ILC3 contributed to the cervical alveolar bone resorption interfacing the gingival inflammation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing bone loss in different knockout mouse models (Figure 8).

claim: The oral mucosa is one of the most active barrier tissues in the human body.
source: The oral mucosa is one of the most active barrier tissues in the human body (Abusleme et al., 2013; Belkaid and Harrison, 2017), and oral barrier immunity acts as a crucial surveillance system to achieve the homeostasis (Moutsopoulos and Moutsopoulos, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Oral barrier immunity acts as a crucial surveillance system to achieve homeostasis.
source: The oral mucosa is one of the most active barrier tissues in the human body (Abusleme et al., 2013; Belkaid and Harrison, 2017), and oral barrier immunity acts as a crucial surveillance system to achieve the homeostasis (Moutsopoulos and Moutsopoulos, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Once gingival inflammation progresses, connective tissues supporting the cervical area of the dentition are subjected to localized and severe degeneration, resulting in tooth loss and disruption of the maxillofacial structure.
source: However, once the gingival inflammation progresses, connective tissues supporting the cervical area of the dentition are subjected to a localized and severe degeneration, resulting in tooth loss and disruption of the maxillofacial structure (Lamont et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Periodontitis is the most frequent cause of tooth loss in adults.
source: Periodontitis is not only the most frequent cause of tooth loss in adults (Helal et al., 2019), but also, globally, ranks among the most significant contributors to poor health and decreased quality of life, imposing substantial economic and healthcare burdens (Peres et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Periodontitis globally ranks among the most significant contributors to poor health and decreased quality of life, imposing substantial economic and healthcare burdens.
source: Periodontitis is not only the most frequent cause of tooth loss in adults (Helal et al., 2019), but also, globally, ranks among the most significant contributors to poor health and decreased quality of life, imposing substantial economic and healthcare burdens (Peres et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model has shown abundant recruitment and excessive activation of neutrophils.
source: For example, the ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model has shown the abundant recruitment and excessive activation of neutrophils (Hajishengallis, 2020) and pathological induction of interleukin (IL)-17-secreting proinflammatory effector CD4+ T helper (Th)17 cells (Hasiakos et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model has shown pathological induction of interleukin (IL)-17-secreting proinflammatory effector CD4+ T helper (Th)17 cells.
source: For example, the ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model has shown the abundant recruitment and excessive activation of neutrophils (Hajishengallis, 2020) and pathological induction of interleukin (IL)-17-secreting proinflammatory effector CD4+ T helper (Th)17 cells (Hasiakos et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pathological immune cells activate osteoclasts, leading to induction of periodontal alveolar bone resorption.
source: It has been hypothesized that these pathological immune cells activate osteoclasts, leading to induction of periodontal alveolar bone resorption (Cekici et al., 2014; Sokol and Luster, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chemokines are involved in the trafficking and activation of inflammatory cells during both homeostasis and disease-associated inflammation.
source: Prior studies have shown that chemokines are involved in the trafficking and activation of inflammatory cells during both homeostasis and disease-associated inflammation (Sokol and Luster, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Chemokines containing disulfide cysteine–cysteine (CC) and cysteine–X–cysteine (CXC) molecular signatures act as ligands for cellular receptors that modulate inflammatory signaling pathways.
source: Chemokines containing disulfide cysteine–cysteine (CC) and cysteine–X–cysteine (CXC) molecular signatures act as ligands for cellular receptors that modulate inflammatory signaling pathways (Hughes and Nibbs, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In addition to immune cells, barrier tissue stromal cells are involved in innate immune cell regulation.
source: However, increasing evidence suggests that in addition to immune cells, barrier tissue stromal cells are involved in innate immune cell regulation (Hodzic et al., 2017; Ina et al., 2005; Pinchuk et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Oral fibroblasts secrete cytokines and chemokines in response to microbial stimuli or to a proinflammatory environment.
source: It has been reported that oral fibroblasts secrete cytokines and chemokines in response to microbial stimuli or to a proinflammatory environment (Kondo et al., 2022; Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The alveolar bone and gingival tissue surrounding the maxillary second molar of C57BL/6J mice presented healthy connective tissue supporting the dentition with minimal CD45+ immune cell infiltration and well-developed collagen architecture on day 0.
source: The alveolar bone and gingival tissue surrounding the maxillary second molar of C57BL/6J mice presented healthy connective tissue supporting the dentition with minimal CD45+ immune cell infiltration and well-developed collagen architecture (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The placement of a ligature around the maxillary left second molar induced a localized and small gingival connective tissue degradation and infiltration of CD45+ immune cells near the cervical area on day 1.
source: The placement of a ligature around the maxillary left second molar (Abe and Hajishengallis, 2013) induced a localized and small gingival connective tissue degradation and infiltration of CD45+ immune cells near the cervical area (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Noticeable gingival defect and more prominent though still localized CD45+ immune cell infiltration developed after day 3 following ligature placement.
source: The noticeable gingival defect and more prominent though still localized CD45+ immune cell infiltration developed after day 3 following ligature placement (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: On day 7, the gingival connective tissue was largely degraded, and chronic inflammation was developed.
source: On day 7, the gingival connective tissue was largely degraded, and chronic inflammation was developed (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1D and supplementary figures.

claim: Three-dimensional reconstruction of micro-computed tomography images revealed a reduction in alveolar bone height starting from day 3, which progressively increased on day 7.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of micro-computed tomography (microCT) images (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) further revealed a reduction in alveolar bone height starting from day 3, which progressively increased on day 7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by microCT imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observed pattern of periodontal tissue degradation was consistent with that reported in previous studies.
source: Overall, the observed pattern of periodontal tissue degradation was consistent with that reported in previous studies (Tamura et al., 2021; Marchesan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature.

claim: Two distinct subpopulations of gingival fibroblasts were previously identified, differentiated by expression of type XIV collagen (Col14a1).
source: We previously identified two distinct subpopulations of gingival fibroblasts, differentiated by expression of type XIV collagen (Col14a1) (Kondo et al., 2022), and these were also detected in our current scRNA-seq data from days 0–7 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This refers to a previous study by the authors and is confirmed in the current scRNA-seq data.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of the Col14a1-expressing fibroblast subpopulation revealed expression of major gene clusters related to immune regulation, including 'Regulation of leukocyte migration'.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the Col14a1-expressing fibroblast subpopulation revealed expression of major gene clusters related to immune regulation, including 'Regulation of leukocyte migration' (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on computational GO analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The immune regulatory phenotype appears to be unique to Col14a1-expressing fibroblasts.
source: This immune regulatory phenotype appears to be unique to Col14a1-expressing fibroblasts, which are therefore referred to as 'fibroblasts activated to guide leukocyte migration' or AG fibroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the GO analysis comparing AG and KT fibroblasts.

claim: The other subpopulation of Col1a1-expressing fibroblasts appeared to keep typical fibroblastic features.
source: The other subpopulation of Col1a1-expressing fibroblasts appeared to keep typical fibroblastic features and is thus referred to as KT fibroblasts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis showing connective tissue remodeling functions in Figure 2C.

claim: GO analysis suggested that KT fibroblasts primarily maintained connective tissue remodeling but did not express an immune regulatory phenotype.
source: GO analysis suggested that KT fibroblasts primarily maintained connective tissue remodeling but did not express an immune regulatory phenotype.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: An additional fibroblast subpopulation expressing smooth muscle actin alpha 2 (Acta2) was detected on day 7, and these were identified as myofibroblasts.
source: An additional fibroblast subpopulation expressing smooth muscle actin alpha 2 (Acta2) was detected on day 7, and these were identified as myofibroblasts (MF) (Sasaki et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data showing Acta2 expression and supported by a citation.

claim: The proportions of KT and AG fibroblasts were equal on day 0 and on days 1 and 4 after ligature placement.
source: We found that the proportions of KT and AG fibroblasts were equal on day 0 and on days 1 and 4 after ligature placement (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: On day 7, the proportion of AG fibroblasts decreased, and the MF fraction emerged.
source: However, on day 7, the proportion of AG fibroblasts decreased, and the MF fraction emerged (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: AG fibroblasts activated expression of Ccl8, Ccl11, Ccl19, Cxcl1, Cxcl10, and Cxcl12 immediately after ligature placement on days 1 and 4.
source: Results show that AG fibroblasts activated expression of Ccl8, Ccl11, Ccl19, Cxcl1, Cxcl10, and Cxcl12 immediately after ligature placement on days 1 and 4 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Chemokine expression levels decreased on day 7 in AG fibroblasts.
source: Chemokine expression levels then decreased on day 7, suggesting that AG fibroblasts might initiate early leukocyte migration into gingival tissue.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data and leads to an inference about AG fibroblast function.

claim: AG fibroblasts might initiate early leukocyte migration into gingival tissue.
source: Chemokine expression levels then decreased on day 7, suggesting that AG fibroblasts might initiate early leukocyte migration into gingival tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of chemokine expression.

claim: AG fibroblasts displayed temporal activation of Tlr2, Tlr3, and Tlr4 expression on days 1 and 4.
source: We found that AG fibroblasts displayed temporal activation of Tlr2, Tlr3, and Tlr4 expression on days 1 and 4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The TLR downstream genes Myd88, Irak1, Map3k7, and RelA were expressed on days 1 and 4 in AG fibroblasts.
source: Similarly, the TLR downstream genes Myd88, Irak1, Map3k7, and RelA were also expressed on days 1 and 4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AG fibroblasts may guide the establishment of an early inflammatory environment within the gingiva and thereby promote periodontitis pathogenesis.
source: These data suggest that AG fibroblasts may guide the establishment of an early inflammatory environment within the gingiva and thereby promote periodontitis pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of chemokines and TLR-related genes.

claim: COL14A1- and CXCL12-positive AG fibroblasts were detected localized near gingival epithelial cells in the connective tissue papillae and free gingiva, as well as in the cervical zone of the periodontal ligament space on day 1.
source: We detected COL14A1- and CXCL12-positive AG fibroblasts localized near gingival epithelial cells in the connective tissue papillae and free gingiva, as well as in the cervical zone of the periodontal ligament (PDL) space (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The localization pattern of AG fibroblasts appears to be highly suitable for early immune surveillance during periodontitis pathogenesis.
source: We note that this localization pattern of AG fibroblasts appears to be highly suitable for early immune surveillance during periodontitis pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical localization of AG fibroblasts.

claim: AG fibroblasts initially sense the pathological stress including oral microbial stimuli through TLRs and secrete inflammatory signals through chemokine expression.
source: Thus, we have hypothesized that AG fibroblasts initially sense the pathological stress including oral microbial stimuli through TLRs and secrete inflammatory signals through chemokine expression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression of TLRs and chemokines in AG fibroblasts.

claim: The microbial composition of the mouse ligature did not mirror the human oral microbial composition.
source: We previously reported that the microbial composition of the mouse ligature did not mirror the human oral microbial composition (Kondo et al., 2022).
evidence: This refers to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Human oral microbial biofilm, but not planktonic microbes, induced initial gingival tissue degradation in the MTA model.
source: We previously reported that human oral microbial biofilm, but not planktonic microbes, induced initial gingival tissue degradation in the MTA model, suggesting that extracellular components of human oral biofilm could play an important role in the initiation of periodontitis (Kondo et al., 2022).
evidence: This refers to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Extracellular components of human oral biofilm could play an important role in the initiation of periodontitis.
source: We previously reported that human oral microbial biofilm, but not planktonic microbes, induced initial gingival tissue degradation in the MTA model, suggesting that extracellular components of human oral biofilm could play an important role in the initiation of periodontitis (Kondo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference from a previous study by the authors.

claim: CpG ODN induced the expression of cathepsin K in the PDL and gingival connective tissue four days after topical application.
source: CpG ODN induced the expression of cathepsin K (Ctsk) in the PDL and gingival connective tissue (Figure 4C) validating the previous report (Kondo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There were signs of localized Ctsk+ osteoclastic activities on the surface of alveolar bone after CpG ODN application.
source: Furthermore, there were signs of localized Ctsk+ osteoclastic activities on the surface of alveolar bone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The gingival cell composition by scRNA-seq of the MTA of CpG ODN or LPS revealed early stage of gingival inflammation, equivalent to day 1 of the ligature-induced periodontitis model.
source: The scRNA-seq gingival cell composition of the MTA of CpG ODN and LPS indicated the early periodontitis pattern (Figure 4E) consistent with day 1 scRNA-seq of the ligature-induced periodontitis (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on comparison of scRNA-seq data from different models.

claim: The MTA of CpG ODN and LPS identified AG fibroblasts along with KT fibroblasts.
source: The MTA of CpG ODN and LPS identified AG fibroblasts along with KT fibroblasts, whereas the MTA of LPS induced the additional MF (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The MTA of LPS induced myofibroblasts.
source: The MTA of CpG ODN and LPS identified AG fibroblasts along with KT fibroblasts, whereas the MTA of LPS induced the additional MF (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AG fibroblasts activated by the MTA of CpG ODN and LPS expressed CCL and CXCL chemokines.
source: Further analysis demonstrated the expression of CCL and CXCL chemokines by AG fibroblasts activated by the MTA of CpG ODN and LPS (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The scRNA-seq of MTA of CpG ODN did not capture the transcriptional activation of Tlr9.
source: The scRNA-seq of MTA of CpG ODN did not capture the transcriptional activation of Tlr9; however, the downstream effector genes associated with TLR9 such as Myd99, Irak1, and RelA were found to be upregulated in AG fibroblasts (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The downstream effector genes associated with TLR9 such as Myd99, Irak1, and RelA were found to be upregulated in AG fibroblasts in the MTA of CpG ODN.
source: The scRNA-seq of MTA of CpG ODN did not capture the transcriptional activation of Tlr9; however, the downstream effector genes associated with TLR9 such as Myd99, Irak1, and RelA were found to be upregulated in AG fibroblasts (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The MTA of LPS appeared to upregulate Tlr2 and Tlr4 gene transcription of AG fibroblasts and of MF.
source: The MTA of LPS appeared to upregulate Tlr2 and Tlr4 gene transcription of AG fibroblasts and of MF albeit at lesser degrees (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: AG fibroblasts were activated by CpG ODN and LPS through the MTA model.
source: These results indicated that AG fibroblasts were activated by CpG ODN and LPS through the MTA model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MTA model experiments.

claim: The extracellular substances of human oral biofilm such as microbial extracellular DNA and LPS might be an important trigger of gingival inflammation.
source: As such, the extracellular substances of human oral biofilm such as microbial extracellular DNA and LPS might be an important trigger of gingival inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MTA model results.

claim: The infiltration of proinflammatory neutrophils into the gingiva has been extensively characterized in the mouse model of ligature-induced periodontitis.
source: The infiltration of proinflammatory neutrophils into the gingiva has been extensively characterized in the mouse model of ligature-induced periodontitis (Hajishengallis, 2020; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Macrophages expressing cluster of differentiation 86 (Cd86) and integrin subunit alpha X (Itgax) were predominant on day 0 in the myeloid cell fraction from healthy gingiva.
source: Here, we found that macrophages expressing cluster of differentiation 86 (Cd86) (Lam et al., 2014) and integrin subunit alpha X (Itgax) (Agarbati et al., 2021) were predominant on day 0 in the myeloid cell fraction from healthy gingiva (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The proportion of neutrophils expressing CXC motif chemokine receptor (Cxcr2) and G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0s2) increased after ligature placement and during periodontitis development from days 1–7.
source: In contrast, the proportion of neutrophils expressing CXC motif chemokine receptor (Cxcr2) (Hashim et al., 2021) and G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0s2) (Zhang et al., 2017) increased after ligature placement and during periodontitis development from days 1–7 (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting continuous neutrophil infiltration into the early and established gingival lesion.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Continuous neutrophil infiltration occurs into the early and established gingival lesion.
source: In contrast, the proportion of neutrophils expressing CXC motif chemokine receptor (Cxcr2) (Hashim et al., 2021) and G0/G1 switch gene 2 (G0s2) (Zhang et al., 2017) increased after ligature placement and during periodontitis development from days 1–7 (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting continuous neutrophil infiltration into the early and established gingival lesion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increasing proportion of neutrophils over time.

claim: After ligature placement, gingival neutrophils upregulated the expression of triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (Trem1).
source: Moreover, after ligature placement, gingival neutrophils upregulated the expression of triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (Trem1), indicating that these cells are activated and participating in the amplification of inflammatory signals (Bouchon et al., 2000; Dopheide et al., 2013; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Trem1-expressing activated neutrophils are participating in the amplification of inflammatory signals.
source: Moreover, after ligature placement, gingival neutrophils upregulated the expression of triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (Trem1), indicating that these cells are activated and participating in the amplification of inflammatory signals (Bouchon et al., 2000; Dopheide et al., 2013; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an inference based on Trem1 expression and supported by citations.

claim: Trem1-expressing activated neutrophils show upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (Mmp9).
source: Strikingly, the Trem1-expressing activated neutrophils also show upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (Mmp9; Figure 5C)—a protein associated with extracellular matrix degeneration within gingival tissue (Corotti et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Matrix metalloproteinase 9 is a protein associated with extracellular matrix degeneration within gingival tissue.
source: Strikingly, the Trem1-expressing activated neutrophils also show upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (Mmp9; Figure 5C)—a protein associated with extracellular matrix degeneration within gingival tissue (Corotti et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Expression of tumor necrosis factor (Tnf) and transforming growth factor beta 1 (Tgfb1) was detected in both macrophages and neutrophils on day 0 and after ligature placement.
source: We further detected expression of tumor necrosis factor (Tnf) and transforming growth factor beta 1 (Tgfb1) in both macrophages and neutrophils on day 0 and after ligature placement (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Macrophages expressed Ccl2, Ccl9, Cxcl4, and Cxcl6 throughout periodontitis development.
source: Our scRNA-seq analysis revealed that macrophages expressed Ccl2, Ccl9, Cxcl4, and Cxcl6, and neutrophils expressed Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl6, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3 throughout periodontitis development (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Neutrophils expressed Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl6, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3 throughout periodontitis development.
source: Our scRNA-seq analysis revealed that macrophages expressed Ccl2, Ccl9, Cxcl4, and Cxcl6, and neutrophils expressed Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl6, Cxcl2, and Cxcl3 throughout periodontitis development (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Chemokines and cytokines produced by macrophages and neutrophils in inflamed tissue may amplify and polarize the immune response toward chronic gingival inflammation.
source: These data suggest that chemokines and cytokines produced by macrophages and neutrophils in inflamed tissue may amplify and polarize the immune response toward chronic gingival inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemokine expression patterns.

claim: AG fibroblasts may regulate macrophages via the expression Ccl8 and Ccl11, which encode chemokines that can interact with CC chemokine receptors encoded by Ccr2 and Ccr5 in macrophages.
source: Results show that AG fibroblasts may regulate macrophages via the expression Ccl8 and Ccl11, which encode chemokines that can interact with CC chemokine receptors (CCRs) encoded by Ccr2 and Ccr5 in macrophages.
evidence: This is based on computational matching of ligand-receptor pairs from scRNA-seq data.

claim: AG fibroblast-mediated neutrophil regulation may occur through CCL8–CCR1, CXCL1–CXCR2, and CXCL12–CXCR4 interactions.
source: Similarly, gene expression signatures suggest that AG fibroblast-mediated neutrophil regulation may occur through CCL8–CCR1, CXCL1–CXCR2, and CXCL12–CXCR4 interactions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on computational matching of ligand-receptor pairs from scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All chemokine–receptor pairs are expressed throughout periodontitis development.
source: Notably, all chemokine–receptor pairs are expressed throughout periodontitis development, although expression of factors mediating the interaction between AG fibroblasts and macrophages was decreased on day 7.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Expression of factors mediating the interaction between AG fibroblasts and macrophages was decreased on day 7.
source: Notably, all chemokine–receptor pairs are expressed throughout periodontitis development, although expression of factors mediating the interaction between AG fibroblasts and macrophages was decreased on day 7.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: There is a trend toward increasing ligand–target interactions between fibroblasts and myeloid cells from day 1 to day 7.
source: Here, we performed NicheNet analysis to identify potential interactions between gingival fibroblasts and myeloid cells, revealing a trend toward increasing ligand–target interactions between fibroblasts and myeloid cells from day 1 to day 7 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on NicheNet computational analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: On day 1, ligand expression was present primarily in AG fibroblasts.
source: On day 1, ligand expression was present primarily in AG fibroblasts, whereas on day 7, MFs also exhibited prominent ligand expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: On day 7, myofibroblasts also exhibited prominent ligand expression.
source: On day 1, ligand expression was present primarily in AG fibroblasts, whereas on day 7, MFs also exhibited prominent ligand expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both macrophages and neutrophils expressed receptors capable of interacting with AG fibroblast ligands on day 1.
source: Analysis of target gene expression revealed that both macrophages and neutrophils expressed receptors capable of interacting with AG fibroblast ligands on day 1.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: On day 7, receptor expression was almost exclusively present in neutrophils.
source: In contrast, on day 7, receptor expression was almost exclusively present in neutrophils, suggesting that these cells are primarily targeted by MFs and AG fibroblasts at later stages of periodontitis development (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neutrophils are primarily targeted by MFs and AG fibroblasts at later stages of periodontitis development.
source: In contrast, on day 7, receptor expression was almost exclusively present in neutrophils, suggesting that these cells are primarily targeted by MFs and AG fibroblasts at later stages of periodontitis development (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the receptor expression pattern on day 7.

claim: Macrophage-colony stimulating factor (M-CSF), encoded by Csf1, and receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (RANKL), encoded by Tnfsf11, are known to play critical roles in osteoclast induction.
source: Macrophage-colony stimulating factor (M-CSF), encoded by Csf1, and receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand (RANKL), encoded by Tnfsf11, are known to play critical roles in osteoclast induction (Teitelbaum, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the ligature-induced periodontitis model, the expression of M-CSF was detected in various cell types including fibroblasts.
source: We found that in the ligature-induced periodontitis model, the expression of M-CSF was detected in various cell types including fibroblasts (Figure 7A), whereas the RNAKL expression was more restricted to fibroblasts and T cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RANKL expression was more restricted to fibroblasts and T cells in the ligature-induced periodontitis model.
source: We found that in the ligature-induced periodontitis model, the expression of M-CSF was detected in various cell types including fibroblasts (Figure 7A), whereas the RNAKL expression was more restricted to fibroblasts and T cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: AG fibroblasts consistently expressed M-CSF from day 0 to day 7.
source: AG fibroblasts consistently expressed M-CSF from day 0 to day 7 and neutrophils started to express M-CSF on days 4 and 7 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Neutrophils started to express M-CSF on days 4 and 7.
source: AG fibroblasts consistently expressed M-CSF from day 0 to day 7 and neutrophils started to express M-CSF on days 4 and 7 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The expression of RANKL was detected in AG fibroblasts but not in myeloid cells.
source: The expression of RNAKL was detected in AG fibroblasts but not in myeloid cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: T cells and type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3) expressed M-CSF and RANKL.
source: T cells and type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3; see below) were also shown to express M-CSF and RNAKL (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C and D.
